questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In the given cycle $A B C D A$, the heat required for an ideal monoatomic gas will be
questions.solution:
In the given cycle, heat is supplied in process $D$ to A$ at constant volume and in process A to B$ at constant pressure.
$\therefore$ Heat supplied, $Q=n C_V(\Delta T)_{D A}+n C_p(\Delta T)_{A B}$
For an ideal monoatomic gas,
$\begin{aligned}
C_V & =\frac{3}{2} R \text{ and } C_p=\frac{5}{2} R \\
\Rightarrow \quad Q & =\frac{3}{2} n R \Delta T+\frac{5}{2} n R \Delta T \quad[\because n R \Delta T=p \Delta V] \\
& =\frac{3}{2}\left(p_0 V_0\right)+5\left(p_0 V_0\right) \\
& =\frac{13}{2} p_0 V_0
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A gas can be taken from A to B via two different processes $A C B$ and $A D B$. When path $A C B$ is used 60 J of heat flows into the system and 30J of work is done by the system. If path ADB is used work done by the system is 10 J. The heat Flow into the system in path ADB is :
questions.solution: $\triangle \mathrm{U}$ remains same for both paths ACB and ADB $\Delta Q_{A C B}=\Delta W_{A C B}+\Delta U_{A C B}$ $\Rightarrow 60 \mathrm{ J}=30 \mathrm{ J}+\Delta \mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{ACB}} \Rightarrow \mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{ACB}}=30 \mathrm{ J}$ As change in internal energy depends only on initial and final point $\therefore \Delta \mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{ADB}}=\Delta \mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{ACB}}=30 \mathrm{ J}\Delta \mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{ADB}}=\Delta \mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{ADB}}+\Delta \mathrm{W}_{\mathrm{ADB}}=10 \mathrm{ J}+30 \mathrm{ J}=40 \mathrm{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A source supplies heat to a system at the rate of 1000 W. If the system performs work at a rate of 200 W. The rate at which internal energy of the system increases
questions.solution:
Given,
Rate of heat supplied, $\frac{\mathrm{dQ}}{\mathrm{dt}}=1000 \mathrm{ W}$
Rate of work performed, $\frac{\mathrm{dw}}{\mathrm{dt}}=200 \mathrm{ W}$
Using first law of thermodynamics
$d Q=d U+d w
\(\Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{dU}}{\mathrm{dt}}=\frac{\mathrm{dQ}}{\mathrm{dt}}-\frac{\mathrm{dw}}{\mathrm{dt}} \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{dU}}{\mathrm{dt}}=1000-200=800\)$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A hypothetical gas expands adiabatically such that its volume changes from 08 litres to 27 litres. If the ratio of final pressure of the gas to initial pressure of the gas is $\frac{16}{81}$. Then the ratio of $\frac{\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{P}}}{\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{V}}}$ will be.
questions.solution: In adiabatic process$\begin{aligned} \\ & \mathrm{PV}^\gamma=\text{ constant } \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \quad \mathrm{P}_1 \mathrm{ V}_1^\gamma=\mathrm{P}_2 \mathrm{ V}_2^\gamma \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \quad \frac{\mathrm{P}_1}{\mathrm{P}_2}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{V}_2}{\mathrm{ V}_1}\right)^\gamma \Rightarrow \frac{81}{16}=\left(\frac{27}{8}\right)^\gamma \\ \\ & \Rightarrow\left(\frac{9}{4}\right)^2=\left(\frac{9 \times 3}{4 \times 2}\right)^\gamma \Rightarrow\left(\frac{9}{4}\right)^{2-\gamma}=\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^\gamma \\ \\ & \Rightarrow\left(\frac{9}{4}\right)^{2-\gamma}=\left(\frac{9}{4}\right)^{\gamma / 2} \Rightarrow 2-\gamma=\frac{\gamma}{2} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 2=\frac{3}{2} \gamma \Rightarrow \gamma=\frac{4}{3} \\ \end{aligned}$

questions.q: An ideal gas at atmospheric pressure is adiabatically compressed so that its density becomes 32 times of its initial value. If the final pressure of gas is 128 atmospheres, the value of ' $\gamma$ ' of the gas is :
questions.solution: Volume $v=\frac{\mathrm{m}}{d}$ and using $\mathrm{PV}^{\gamma}=$ constant $\begin{array}{l} \frac{\mathrm{P}^{\prime}}{\mathrm{P}}=\frac{\mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{V}^{\prime}}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}^{\prime}}{\mathrm{d}}\right)^{\gamma} \\ \text{ or } 128=(32)^{\gamma} \\ \therefore \gamma=\frac{7}{5}=1.4 \end{array}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An ideal monoatomic gas at $300K$ expands adiabatically to twice its volume. The final temperature of gas is
questions.solution:
For an ideal monatomic gas, the ratio of specific heat capacity at constant pressure to specific heat capacity at constant volume is

$\gamma = \dfrac{5}{3}$

In an adiabatic process,

$TV^{\gamma - 1} =$ constant

i.e. ${T}_{f}{V}_f^{\gamma - 1} = {T}_{i}{V}_i^{\gamma - 1} ⇒ {T}_{f} = {T}_{i}\left(\dfrac{Vi}{Vf}\right)\gamma - 1 = 300\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\dfrac{5}{3} - 1$

$= 300\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2} / 3$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The pressure versus temperature graph of an ideal gas is shown in the figure below. If the density of gas at point $A$ is ${ρ}_{0}$, then the density of the gas at point $B$& will be
questions.solution:
Given, density of gas at point A, {ρ}_{A} = {ρ}_{0}$

General equation for an ideal gas

$pV = nRT$

$⇒ pV = $\dfrac{m}{M}$RT$ [m \to$mass, $M \to$ molecular mass]

$⇒ p = \dfrac{m}{V} \cdot \dfrac{R}{M} \cdot T$

$⇒ p = ρ \left(\dfrac{R}{M}$\right)$T... \left(i\right) & [where density $ρ = $\dfrac{m}{V}$]$

Applying Equation. (i) at point A and B$, respectively.

$p = {ρ}_{A} \left(\dfrac{R}{M}$\right){T}_{0}...$\left(ii\right)$

$2p = {ρ}_{B} \left(\dfrac{R}{M}\right)3{T}_{0}... \left(iii\right)

From Equations. (ii)$ and $(iii), we get

\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{ρA}{ρB} \cdot \dfrac{1}{3}$

$⇒ {ρ}_{B} = \dfrac{2}{3}{ρ}_{A} = \dfrac{2}{3}{ρ}_{0}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Helium gas goes through a cycle $ABCDA$ (consisting of two isochoric and two isobaric lines) as shown in figure. The efficiency of this cycle is approximately
questions.solution:
Helium is mono atomic gas, for which
${C}_{V} = \dfrac{3}{2}R . {C}_{p} = \dfrac{5}{2}R$

Work done by the gas in one complete cycle $W =$ area $ABCDA = {p}_{0}{V}_{0}$

From $A to B$, Heat given to gas $= n{C}_{V}\Delta T$

$= 1 \times \left(\dfrac{3}{2}R\right) \times \Delta T = \dfrac{3}{2}{V}_{0}\left(\Deltap\right) = \dfrac{3}{2}{V}_{0}{p}_{0}$

From $B$~to $C$,~heat given to gas $= n{C}_{p}\Delta T$

$= 1 \times \left(\dfrac{5}{2}R\right) \times \Delta T = \dfrac{5}{2}\left(2{p}_{0}\right)\Delta V = 5{p}_{0}{V}_{0}$

Efficiency of cycle $= \dfrac{Workdonebythegas / cycle}{Totalheatgiventogas / cycle}$

$= \dfrac{{p}_{0}{V}_{0}}{\dfrac{3}{2}{p}_{0}{V}_{0} + 5{p}_{0}{V}_{0}} = \dfrac{2}{13}$

Efficiency $\left(%\right) = \dfrac{2}{13} \times 100 = 15 . 4 %$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A vessel of volume 20L contains a mixture of hydrogen and helium at temperature of $27^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ and pressure 2 atm. The mass of mixture is $5 \mathrm{ g}$. Assuming the gases to be ideal, the ratio of mass of hydrogen to that of helium in the given mixture will be
questions.solution: Let there are $\mathrm{n}_{1}$ moles of hydrogen and $\mathrm{n}_{2}$ moles of helium in the given mixture. As $\mathrm{Pv}=\mathrm{nRT}$ Then the pressure of the mixture $\begin{array}{r}$ P=$\frac{\mathrm{n}_{1} \mathrm{RT}}{\mathrm{V}}+\frac{\mathrm{n}_{2} \mathrm{RT}}{\mathrm{V}}=\left(\mathrm{n}_{1}+\mathrm{n}_{2}\right) \frac{\mathrm{RT}}{\mathrm{V}}$\\ 2 $\times101.3 \times10^{3}=\left(\mathrm{n}_{1}+\mathrm{n}_{2}\right) \times \frac{(8.3 \times 300)}{20 \times 10^{-3}} \end{array}$ or, $\begin{array}{l}\left(\mathrm{n}_{1}+\mathrm{n}_{2}\right)=\frac{2 \times 101.3 \times 10^{3} \times 20 \times 10^{-3}}{(8.3)(300)}$\\ $\text{ or, } \mathrm{n}_{1}+\mathrm{n}_{2}=1.62 \end{array} The mass of the mixture is (in grams) \begin{array}{l}\mathrm{n}_{1} \times2+\mathrm{n}_{2} \times4=5 \\ \Rightarrow \quad\left(\mathrm{n}_{1}+2 \mathrm{n}_{2}\right)=2.5 \quad \ldots \end{array} Solving the eqns. (1) and (2), we get \mathrm{n}_{1}=0.74$ and $\mathrm{n}_{2}=0.88$ Hence, $\frac{\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{H}}}{\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{He}}}=\frac{0.74 \times 2}{0.88 \times 4}=\frac{1.48}{3.52}=\frac{2}{5}$

questions.q: One mole of $\mathrm{O}_{2}$ gas having a volume equal to 22.4 Litres at $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and 1 atmospheric pressure in compressed isothermally so that its volume reduces to 11.2 litres. The work done in this process is-
questions.solution:
Work done in adiabatic process, \(\mathrm{W}=\mu \mathrm{RT} \log _{\mathrm{e}}\left(\frac{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{f}}}{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{i}}}\right)\)

\(\mathrm{W}=1 \times 8.314 \times 273 \times \log _{\mathrm{e}}\left(\frac{11.2}{22.4}\right)\)

\(\mathrm{W}=8.314 \times 273 \times \log _{\mathrm{e}}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\)

\(\mathrm{W}=8.314 \times 273 \times\left[\log _{\mathrm{e}}(1)-\log _{\mathrm{e}}(2)\right]\)

\(\mathrm{W}=8.314 \times 273 \times(0-0.69)\)

\(\mathrm{W}=-1566.1 \mathrm{~J}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A Carnot's heat engine works between the temperatures $427^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ and $27^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$. What amount of heat should it consume per second to deliver mechanical work at the rate of $1.0 \mathrm{ kW} ?$
questions.solution: The efficiency of the heat engine is \eta=1-$\frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}}=1-\left(\frac{273+27 K}{273+427 K}\right)=\frac{4}{7}$ But $\quad \eta=\frac{\mathrm{W}}{\mathrm{Q}_{1}}$ \therefore $\mathrm{Q}_{1}=\frac{\mathrm{W}}{\eta}=\frac{1.0 \mathrm{ kW}}{4 / 7}=1.75 \mathrm{ kW}=0.417 \mathrm{kcal}$/ $\mathrm{s}$ Thus, the engine would require 417 cal of heat per second, to deliver the requisite amount of work.

questions.q: A vessel containing 1 more of $\mathrm{O}_{2}$ gas (molar mass 32) at temperature $\mathrm{T}$. The pressure of the gas is p. An identical vessel containing one mole of he gas (molar mass 4 ) at temperature $2 \mathrm{ T}$ has a pressure of

questions.q: Two gases occupy two containers $A$ and $B$ the gas in $\mathrm{A},$ of volume $0.10 \mathrm{ m}^{3},$ exerts a pressure of $1.40 \mathrm{MPa}$ and that in $\mathrm{B}$ of volume $0.15 \mathrm{ m}^{3}$ exerts a pressure $0.7 \mathrm{MPa}$. The two containers are united by a tube of negligible volume and the gases are allowed to intermingle. Then if the temperature remains constant, the final pressure in the container will be (in MPa)
questions.solution: We know that $\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{A}} \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{A}}=\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{A}} \mathrm{RT}, \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{B}} \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{B}}=\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{B}} \mathrm{RT}\begin{array}{ll} & \text{ and } P_{f}\left(V_{A}+V_{B}\right)=\left(n_{A}+n_{B}\right) R T \\ & P_{f}\left(V_{A}+V_{B}\right)=P_{A} V_{A}+P_{B} V_{B} \\ \therefore & P_{f}=\left(\frac{P_{A} V_{A}+P_{B} V_{B}}{V_{A}+V_{B}}\right) \\ & =\frac{1.4 \times 0.1+0.7 \times 0.15}{0.1+0.15} \mathrm{MPa}=0.98 \mathrm{MPa}\end{array}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A cyclic process is shown in the p-T diagram. Which of the curves show the same process on a $\mathrm{P}$ - $\mathrm{V}$ diagram?
questions.solution:
- Given diagram: P-T graph.
- Using ideal gas law: \(P V=n R T \Rightarrow V=$\frac{n R T}{P}$.
So in a \(P-T\) graph we can infer how \(V\) behaves.
Step analysis of cycle \($\mathrm{A} \rightarrow \mathrm{B} \rightarrow \mathrm{C} \rightarrow \mathrm{A}$ :
- A \($\rightarrow \mathrm{B}: Both \(P\) and $\(T\) increase proportionally (straight line through origin).
\(\Rightarrow V=\frac{n R T}{P}$=$\text{ constant. }$
So \($\mathrm{A}$ \rightarrow $\mathrm{B}$ is an isochoric process in \(P-V\).
- \($\mathrm{B}$ \rightarrow $\mathrm{C}$: T\) constant, \(P\) decreases.
\(\Rightarrow\) Isothermal expansion$ in \(P-V\).
- \(\mathrm{C} \rightarrow\mathrm{A}: P\) constant, \(T\) decreases.
\(\Rightarrow\) Isochoric process in \(P-V\).
So the cycle consists of:
- Isochoric line,
- Isothermal curve,
- Isochoric line.
This matches diagram (2).
